A single mongod is a single point of failure. A replica set is a group of mongod processes that maintain copies of the same data and automatically elect a new primary when one fails. Three or more members get you durability, automatic failover, optional read scaling on secondaries, and zero-downtime maintenance. This post covers the architecture, the oplog, election protocol, write-concern interaction with replication, secondary read trade-offs, and the canonical 3-member + arbiter topologies.

Three things at once:
Durability — N copies of the data; loss of one server doesn't lose data.
High availability — automatic failover; clients reconnect to a new primary in seconds.
Read scaling (optional) — secondaries serve eventual-consistent reads.
Replication doesn't scale writes — every write still goes through one primary. For write scaling, you shard (Post 11) on top of replica sets.

Role · Receives writes · Serves reads · Votes in election · Holds data
PRIMARY · yes (only one at a time) · yes · yes · yes
SECONDARY · replicates from primary's oplog · yes (with secondaryPreferred etc.) · yes · yes
ARBITER · no · no · yes · no — voting only
HIDDEN · no · no (invisible to drivers) · yes · yes (backups, analytics)
DELAYED · no · no · yes · yes (lags primary by N seconds — disaster recovery)
A typical minimal production set: 3 data-bearing members (1 primary + 2 secondaries). Loss of any one keeps a majority alive.
Avoid:
Even number of voting members without an arbiter → election can split. Always odd.
Arbiter-only failover safety in 2026 → arbiters can't vote on majority writes; prefer a 3-data-member setup unless cost-constrained. (See "election + write concern" pitfall in Chapter 8.)

# start three mongod instances on different ports
mkdir -p data/rs0-{0,1,2}
mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27017 --dbpath data/rs0-0 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --fork --logpath data/rs0-0/log
mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27018 --dbpath data/rs0-1 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --fork --logpath data/rs0-1/log
mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27019 --dbpath data/rs0-2 --bind_ip 127.0.0.1 --fork --logpath data/rs0-2/log
Connect to one + initiate:
mongosh --port 27017
rs.initiate({
_id: "rs0",
members: [
{ _id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27017" },
{ _id: 1, host: "127.0.0.1:27018" },
{ _id: 2, host: "127.0.0.1:27019" }
]
})
rs.status()
rs.conf()
Within a second or two, one member is PRIMARY, the other two are SECONDARY.
In Atlas, every cluster is already a replica set — you don't initiate manually.

mongodb://host1:27017,host2:27017,host3:27017/?replicaSet=rs0
mongodb+srv://cluster.abcd.mongodb.net/?retryWrites=true # SRV form, Atlas
The driver:
Reads the seed list (your hosts).
Polls each to discover the full topology and the current primary.
Re-discovers automatically on failover.
You only need to list a few seed hosts — the driver finds the rest. The SRV form (Atlas) returns the full member list via DNS, so the URI stays short.

The oplog is a capped collection (local.oplog.rs) on every replica-set member that records every write applied. Secondaries tail it and replay it to stay in sync.
use local
db.oplog.rs.find().sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(5)
Each entry: timestamp, operation type (insert/update/delete), namespace, document or update spec.

Default size: 5 % of free disk (with a 50 GB upper cap on most platforms). If a secondary falls behind by more oplog entries than fit, it goes STALE and must do a full resync — slow.
Tune via --oplogSizeMB at start, or replSetResizeOplog admin command. Atlas auto-sizes.
Trick: if you regularly run multi-hour ingest jobs while secondaries catch up, increase oplog size. The "1 day of writes fits" rule of thumb prevents most stale-member surprises.

Client writes to PRIMARY.
PRIMARY records the write to its own oplog and applies it.
Each SECONDARY tails the primary's oplog and applies in order.
Once a majority of voters have applied the write, it's "majority committed".
Replication lag = how far behind the primary a secondary is in oplog time.
Inspect:
rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()
// returns each secondary's lag in seconds
Causes of lag:
Big write spike (secondaries can't keep up).
Slow disk on a secondary.
Network latency (especially across regions).
Long oplog entries (huge updates).
Persistent lag > a few seconds = warning. Lag growing unbounded = crisis (eventually goes STALE).

If the PRIMARY becomes unreachable, voting members hold an election (under the hood: Raft-like protocol Version 1, "PV1").
Steps:
A secondary that hasn't heard from the primary for electionTimeoutMillis (default 10 s) calls an election.
Other voting members vote yes if the candidate's oplog is up-to-date enough.
Majority of votes → new PRIMARY.
Drivers detect the change via heartbeats; subsequent writes go to the new primary.
Typical failover: 10-20 seconds for clients to reconnect; retryable writes (Post 08) hide most of the disruption.

rs.stepDown(60) // current primary steps down for 60 s
A useful production drill — practise failover under controlled conditions.

Recap from Post 08 — write concern interacts with replication:
w · Meaning
0 · fire-and-forget
1 · primary acked
"majority" · majority of voters acked
N · exactly N members acked
"majority" is the production-correct default — guarantees the write survives the primary failing (because at least one surviving voter has it).

If you have a 2-data + 1-arbiter set (total 3 voters, majority = 2), arbiters can vote in elections but don't store data. A write reaching only the primary + the arbiter (waiting for the second data member) can be lost in failover. Modern guidance: avoid arbiters in 2026 for any system where data loss isn't acceptable. Use 3 data-bearing members.

Recap from Post 08:
Preference · Effect
primary (default) · always primary, freshest
primaryPreferred · primary if up, else secondary
secondary · secondary only
secondaryPreferred · secondary first, fall back to primary
nearest · lowest-latency member
Use secondary reads for:
Reporting / dashboards tolerating seconds of lag.
Scaling read-heavy workloads horizontally.
Region-local reads via tagSets.
Don't use for:
Read-your-own-writes (RYOW) without causal-consistency session.
Anything where stale-by-seconds matters (orders, balances, leaderboards).

Each member has a configuration in rs.conf():
const cfg = rs.conf();
cfg.members[1].priority = 0; // never become primary
cfg.members[1].hidden = true; // invisible to drivers (analytics replica)
cfg.members[1].slaveDelay = 3600; // older Mongo; modern uses secondaryDelaySecs
rs.reconfig(cfg);
Common variations:
Analytics replica — hidden, priority 0 → drivers never route reads here; you connect directly for heavy analytics queries.
Backup target — hidden, priority 0 → take snapshots without affecting production reads.
Delayed member — secondaryDelaySecs: 3600 → lags primary by 1 hour. Disaster recovery against fat-finger drops ("oops, restore from the delayed member's state of an hour ago").

m1: data, primary candidate (priority 1)
m2: data, primary candidate (priority 1) — different AZ
m3: data, primary candidate (priority 1) — third AZ
m4: data, hidden, priority 0 — analytics replica
m5: data, hidden, priority 0, secondaryDelaySecs: 3600 — DR replica
5 voters (majority 3). Tolerates 2 simultaneous failures of voting members.

Topology · Voters · Majority · Tolerated failures · When
3 data · 3 · 2 · 1 · minimum production
2 data + 1 arbiter · 3 · 2 · 1 · cheap; avoid in 2026
5 data · 5 · 3 · 2 · larger production, mixed roles
7 data · 7 · 4 · 3 · very high availability; rare
3 data, multi-region · 3 · 2 · 1 (region) · DR; read latency increases; needs tagSets
Voters max is 7 in a replica set (additional members can be non-voting).
Multi-region replica set: one primary serves global writes, secondaries in other regions serve local reads. Trade-off: writes to a "far" primary have high latency. Sharding by region (Post 11) often beats multi-region replica sets for writes.

rs.freeze(seconds) // prevent this member from being elected

To upgrade or restart members without downtime:
Pick a secondary. Drain its connections.
Stop + upgrade + restart it. Wait for SECONDARY state.
Repeat for the next secondary.
Step down the primary (rs.stepDown()); it becomes secondary; another member becomes primary.
Stop + upgrade + restart the old primary. Wait for SECONDARY.
Zero downtime as long as a majority is always up. This is the "rolling upgrade" pattern for any major version bump or OS patch.
Atlas does this automatically when you click "Upgrade".

Symptom · Cause · Fix
Failover takes 30+ seconds · electionTimeoutMillis too high; or driver serverSelectionTimeoutMS too high · lower both modestly; test
Secondaries falling behind · undersized oplog or slow disk on secondary · enlarge oplog; faster disk
Stale secondary · lag exceeded oplog window · full resync; or enlarge oplog
Data lost after failover · used w: 1 instead of w: "majority" · switch to majority
Even number of voters · possible split-brain · add an arbiter or another data member
Arbiter loses data (2+1 set) · known antipattern · use 3 data members
Driver doesn't see new primary · replicaSet= missing or wrong; DNS slow · check connection string; SRV form preferred
Cross-region writes slow · primary is far from app · route writes to local primary or shard by region
Secondary read returns stale doc · replication lag · use causal consistency session or primary
Initiate the 3-node set from Chapter 3. Insert data. Confirm replication: read on secondary (allow db.getMongo().setReadPref('secondaryPreferred')).
Run rs.stepDown(30). Watch a Node script that does inserts every second — note the brief failure + resume (retryable writes save the day).
use local; db.oplog.rs.find().sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(10). Identify your last few writes.
In one window, run a tight insert loop. In another, stop one secondary (mongod SIGSTOP / pause). Restart it after a minute. Watch rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo() show the catch-up.
Set member 2 to priority: 0, hidden: true. Confirm drivers no longer route reads there. Connect directly to that member for heavy aggregations.
Configure member 2 with secondaryDelaySecs: 60. Insert a doc. Immediately read from member 2 (direct connection) — should not see it. Wait 90 s, read again — should see it.
